title: Should we Shoot Down UFOs?
byline: Michael Bohlander - 30 September 2026 International law and human rights
excerpt: Michael Bohlander looks at what the existing rules on civilian and military aircraft imply for unidentified anomalous phenomena, and argues that in the absence of evidence of hostile intent, the default should be protection rather than destruction.
content:
Michael Bohlander looks at what the existing rules on civilian and military aircraft imply for unidentified anomalous phenomena, and argues that in the absence of evidence of hostile intent, the default should be protection rather than destruction.

In February 2023, a Chinese spy balloon was shot down over South Carolina. This was followed by three other objects which, however, reportedly flew without any apparent propulsion system. They were also shot down. The head of NORAD stated that he was “not going to categorise them as balloons. We’re calling them objects for a reason.” He specifically did not initially rule out an extraterrestrial origin, either. Recordings of the pilots’ conversations engaging the third object over Lake Huron on 12 February 2023 showed their uncertainty as to how to classify it. These events followed other encounters such as the ones in 2004 with the USS Nimitz carrier strike group or the 2015 USS Roosevelt encounter. They are part of a wider development described by military and civilian pilots reporting objects which defy identification and the known laws of physics. During a congressional hearing on unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) in 2025, a video was shown of US drones attacking a UAP with a Hellfire missile with little effect. 

Which legal framework is relevant to determining whether the destruction of UAP is permitted, whether on land, sea, or in the air? Is it possible to establish general principles based on the rules applicable in peacetime or war? The publicly known and observable UAP behaviour makes it difficult to classify them (all) unambiguously as military, civilian, or something in between, or whether they are hostile or benevolent. This post gives a brief overview of some relevant considerations. 

Possible factual scenarios

A UAP could be a (secret) human military or a civilian object. It may belong to a state or a citizen of a state over which it is detected, or it may have had permission of overflight. This could be deduced from transponder signals, nationality markings, or other decals human craft must display. Human origin might be excluded by extraordinary displays of capacities clearly pointing to a non-human origin of the technology. Finally, it is important whether there is a crew of biological entities on board. It may be permissible to shoot down a machine, but not living beings. In reality, this will be very difficult to ascertain due to both government secrecy and the elusive nature of the UAP. 

The law

There is little hope of any open official discussion of principled legal thinking about destroying non-human UAP. There is no transparency about any Rules of Engagement (RoE) to begin with. The planned research exercise based on the paper “UK readiness for black swan scientific events: Case Study – The discovery of life beyond Earth” by the UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology from 2023 was paused indefinitely in the second half of 2024. The US intelligence community has an iron grip on the entire UAP environment and seems unwilling to relinquish control. We will thus have to rely on general inter-human regulations and extrapolate. The main distinction relevant for our purposes is between civilian and military objects. However, modern technology has made this distinction difficult. One example are unmarked drones of state and non-state actors, which carry no transponder that would allow such a classification. Even mere human drone activity seems far from being well-regulated under international or  domestic law.

Civilian nature

Attacking civilian aircraft is as a rule prohibited under the Convention on International Civil Aviation of 7 December 1944. A similar result follows from the application of international humanitarian law on the protection of civilians from war crimes or crimes against humanity. However, as state practice has shown, the rule about civilian craft is not considered absolute, especially if serious risks might arise from a civilian aircraft that poses an actual threat akin to a military one, as exemplified by the attacks with civilian planes on the World Trade Centre and the Pentagon on 11 September 2001. Yet, such a view is not uniformly held, either, and domestic protections may have a wider reach, as demonstrated by the 2006 decision of the German Federal Constitutional Court which partially struck down the Air Traffic Security Act 2005 as unconstitutional, section 14(3) of which would have allowed “[t]he direct use of weapons … only … if under the circumstances it must be assumed that the airplane will be used against the lives of human beings and that such use is the only means of averting that present danger.” (my translation).

Military nature

Assuming a UAP is non-human and of a military nature and especially if it behaves in a hostile manner, the rules might shift to a lower threshold for reaction in line with general military or even law enforcement rules, such as, for example, the RoE, the general law of armed conflict, and the law of self-defence, or general public order policing laws. However, the relationship between these is again anything but well-delineated. The US military in particular seems to consider such concerns irrelevant. This is amply illustrated by the above-mentioned attack on what was very likely a legitimate candidate for a non-human UAP. The object was travelling over non-US territory, displaying no threat or hostility, and still the US fired a Hellfire missile at it. The effect of the strike was negligible. The object continued on its course with a few minor pieces of debris continuing to fly along on the same trajectory, making it even  more probable that it was highly advanced technology.

Transferring concepts and distinction in practice

Can we transfer the civilian/military distinction to non-human species who might be behind  UAP? Can we know if the UAP is crewed or not? Much may depend on whether they display any threat or hostile intentions. The record of the UAP observed so far is mostly pointing towards purely defensive action, mainly either evading human weapon systems by outrunning them through sheer speed or superior manoeuvring capabilities, by employing defence mechanisms rendering them ineffective even if  hitting their target, or by disabling weapon guidance systems. Incidents of aggressive behaviour initiated by UAP are very rare. A clear verdict of a military nature or threat will thus be very difficult to reach in virtually all cases, an argument in favour of classifying UAP by default as non-aggressive and falling under the same protection as human civilian objects. They should not be attacked, unless they show hostile intent.

Conclusion

While the behaviour of the UAP observed to date tends to support an overall non-aggressive nature – excluding, of course, reports of abductions – prior state practice of engaging them is proof that governments are not prepared to abide by this realisation and opt instead for views based on a default characterisation as a general threat and on an enforcement of territoriality or other state interests. Any efforts towards an international consensus are therefore currently bound to fall prey to geopolitical and -strategic parameters. The wisdom of the current attitude is moreover rather doubtful: While UAP so far seem to have been restrained in their reaction to human aggressive behaviour, there is no guarantee that this will continue to be the case, for example, if the attack was not against a small, unmanned probe, but against one of the larger observed craft that may well be carrying crew. Some of them may carry weapon systems equally advanced as their overall technology. We should not test them without good reason and a colourable case that we would prevail.

Dr Michael Bohlander holds the Chair in Global Law and SETI Policy in Durham Law School in the United Kingdom.

This post is based on a chapter entitled “Destroying non-human unidentified anomalous phenomena – A chance for regulation or a perennial legal black box?”, forthcoming in 2027 in a book about the future research agenda for international criminal law, edited by Anna Marie Brennan.
